clinical_knowledge.topic: Knee Osteoarthritis (rehabilitation focus) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Knee Osteoarthritis (rehabilitation focus) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes a structured weight-loss program, physical therapy focused on quadriceps strengthening, and topical NSAIDs, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: knee pain on stairs, morning stiffness <30 minutes

Key HPI features: A 44-year-old female presents to the clinic with knee pain on stairs, morning stiffness <30 minutes. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Bony crepitus and tenderness along the joint line, no erythema or warmth, no significant effusion; weight-bearing X-ray shows joint space narrowing.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Knee Osteoarthritis (rehabilitation focus).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Rheumatoid arthritis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Hot, red, swollen joint or fever — suggests septic or inflammatory arthritis rather than osteoarthritis.
management_principles: Plan for Knee Osteoarthritis rehab: Weight loss program, physical therapy for quadriceps, topical NSAID
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of knee pain on stairs, morning stiffness <30 minutes. HPI: Gradually worsening knee pain worse with stair climbing, morning stiffness lasting under 30 minutes, no trauma or joint swelling.
reference_soap.objective: Bony crepitus and joint-line tenderness, no erythema, warmth, or significant effusion; weight-bearing X-ray shows joint space narrowing consistent with osteoarthritis.
reference_soap.assessment: Knee osteoarthritis, given activity-related pain, brief morning stiffness under 30 minutes, and crepitus without inflammatory signs.
reference_soap.plan: Plan for Knee Osteoarthritis rehab: Weight loss program, physical therapy for quadriceps, topical NSAID. Consult specialist if symptoms worsen. Counsel patient.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Knee Osteoarthritis rehab
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Knee Osteoarthritis rehab
Implement evidence-based management plan: Weight loss program, physical therapy for quadriceps, topical NSAID

teaching.one_liner: Knee pain worse with stairs and brief morning stiffness, managed with weight loss, physical therapy, and topical NSAIDs.
red_flags: Hot, red, swollen joint or fever — suggests septic or inflammatory arthritis rather than osteoarthritis
Significant trauma with inability to bear weight — needs imaging to exclude fracture
Locking or giving way with a large effusion — consider mechanical internal derangement (meniscal tear)
